claims.text: Phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys is governed by the degree of chemical short-range order.
Atomic-size mismatch and chemical-enthalpy differences among the constituent elements induce chemical short-range order.
Al has an especially important role in governing short-range order in this alloy system.
Increasing the local Al concentration promotes chemical short-range order.
Al-promoted short-range order nucleates B2-type ordered regions within a BCC matrix.
Increasing Al stabilizes BCC/B2 relative to FCC and shifts the phase balance toward a higher BCC/B2 fraction.
BCC/B2 regions provide greater high-temperature strength than the FCC-dominated state.
BCC/B2 regions provide improved oxidation resistance.
BCC/B2 regions provide improved radiation tolerance.
FCC regions are critical for cryogenic toughness.
Increasing the BCC/B2 fraction will reduce cryogenic toughness relative to an FCC-dominated baseline.
The baseline balanced Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy is predominantly FCC with a minority BCC/B2 fraction.
The proposed mechanism applies under processing conditions that permit equilibrium or near-equilibrium phase formation.
The effect is limited to an Al range that promotes short-range order without causing excessive brittleness or other detrimental microstructural features.
The proposed Al effect is bounded to comparisons in which the ratios of Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni are fixed.
